We discuss the synchrotron emission of fast cooling electrons in shocks. The fast cooling electrons behind the shocks can generate a position-dependent inhomogeneous electron distribution if they do not have enough time to mix homogeneously. This would lead to a very different synchrotron spectrum in low-frequency bands to that in the homogeneous case due to the synchrotron absorption. In this paper, we calculate the synchrotron spectrum in the inhomogeneous case in a gamma-ray burst (GRB). Both the forward shock and the reverse shock are considered. We find for the reverse shock dominated case, we would expect a "reverse shock bump" in the low-frequency spectrum. The spectral bump is due to the combination synchrotron absorption in both the forward and reverse shock regions.

We also find that the bump position and amplitude depend on the shock parameters, such as the magnetic field strength and the electron injection index, as well as on the observing time. In particular, the bump becomes more prominent at earlier times and shifts toward lower frequencies as the shock evolves. For the forward shock dominated case, the inhomogeneous distribution leads to a softer low-frequency spectrum compared to the homogeneous case, which may be tested by current and future radio observations of GRBs. Our results suggest that the inhomogeneous electron distribution behind shocks can significantly affect the low-frequency synchrotron emission, and should be taken into account when interpreting broadband afterglow data.

A restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) is an undirected graphical model constructed for discrete or continuous random variables, with two layers, one hidden and one visible, and no conditional dependency within a layer. In recent years, RBMs have risen to prominence due to their connection to deep learning. By treating a hidden layer of one RBM as the visible layer in a second RBM, a deep architecture can be created.

This stacking process can be iterated to build deep belief networks (DBNs), which have demonstrated remarkable performance in tasks like image and speech recognition. The training of an RBM typically involves contrastive divergence, an approximation algorithm that efficiently learns the weights between the visible and hidden layers. Unlike feedforward networks, RBMs learn the joint probability distribution of their inputs, making them particularly useful for collaborative filtering and dimensionality reduction. Their generative nature allows them to model complex data distributions, such as natural images or sequential data, with fewer labeled examples than discriminative models.

Let $G$ be a directed graph on finitely many vertices and edges, and assign a positive weight to each edge on $G$. Fix vertices $u$ and $v$ and consider the set of paths that start at $u$ and end at $v$, self-intersecting in any number of places along the way. For each path, sum the weights of its edges, and then list the path weights in increasing order.

Because the graph is finite and every edge has positive weight, only finitely many paths can have weight at most any given bound: any path exceeding $|V|-1$ edges must repeat a vertex, and the repeated cycle contributes positive weight each time it is traversed. Hence the list of path weights is a discrete multiset with no accumulation point except at infinity. In particular, the smallest entry in the list exists and equals the shortest-path distance from $u$ to $v$ in the usual sense. The second-smallest entry, when the list contains at least two paths, is the subject of what follows: we call it the second shortest-path distance, and we ask how it behaves when the shortest path is removed from the graph, or when an edge along it is perturbed.

As I grew older and slowly understood how Grandfather lived his life, I began to follow in his footsteps. He protected nature’s beauty from decay with his art, and in the same way, I tried to protect my relationships, my artwork, and my memories. I surrounded myself with the journals we wrote together, but this time I recorded my own accomplishments, hoping to one day show him what I had done. I recorded everything, from the first time I spent a week away from home to the time I received a gold medal at the top of the podium at the California Tae Kwon Do Competition. I filled my new home in America with the photographs from my childhood and began to create art of my own. Instead of catching butterflies like my grandpa, I began experimenting with butterfly wing art as my way of preserving nature’s beauty.

My canvases became a refuge for their fragile brilliance, each wing pressed gently into resin or paint, their colors immortalized in a stillness they never knew in life. I would spend hours hunched over my desk, tweezers in hand, arranging their delicate forms into patterns that echoed the hillside of my memory. Friends would ask why I didn’t simply take photographs, and I would smile, unable to explain that a photograph captures light, but this—this captured a moment, a breath, a life that had once trembled against my palm. It was my grandfather’s voice I heard each time I sealed a wing beneath glass, reminding me that beauty, however brief, deserved to be remembered.

The years slipped by like butterflies on a breeze. I graduated, found work, fell in love, and lost it, and through it all, my art remained my constant companion. I began to exhibit my pieces in small galleries, and strangers would pause before them, their faces softening with wonder. Some would ask where I drew my inspiration, and I would tell them about a man with calloused hands and a gentle heart, a man who taught me that holding on too tightly only hastened the end. I wrote him letters, though I never sent them, describing my shows, my successes, my quiet failures. I imagined him reading them aloud to the mountains, his laughter echoing through the pines.

Then came the call I had always dreaded. My mother’s voice, thin and far away, told me that Grandfather was gone. My guide points out the areas where the grass is overgrown and the fruit trees abundant. People and animals alike know to avoid them; someone has learned of landmines the hard way. It shouldn’t surprise me — the scars of war on this rugged country are omnipresent — but it is so jarringly different from my life in London that it is nevertheless hard to digest. It also differs from my father’s rosy stories about his childhood in Katyr-Yurt, stories that made me wish to swim carefree in icy rivers, devour handfuls of fresh sour cherries straight from the tree, and see nights dense with stars. I still experience these beauties of place, but my eyes are now open to the less romanticized parts, both enriching and complicating my connection to my family’s past. Suddenly, too, I am made uncomfortably aware of the conflicting layers of my familial identity. It is the Russian of my Muscovite, Jewish mother that I grew up speaking at home. Yet the Chechen children speak in broken Russian, and the grownups who are more fluent in it are not keen to communicate in the enemy’s language. Seeing the ugly scars of war, both physical and psychological, I cannot help but feel like an intruder, ashamed not only of my Russianness but also of my city-boy naivete. Despite this shame, I yearn to discover what it means to be Chechen, to see their home through their eyes, and through this desire, I begin to feel a deep connection all of my own to this beautiful, fraught land.

...as if sensing my turmoil, the boy takes my hand and leads me down a narrow path, where the wildflowers grow so thick they nearly obscure the ground. He points to a cluster of purple thyme and says, almost proudly, that his grandmother uses it to make tea when the nights grow cold. I bend to smell it, and he laughs—this is the first time he’s ever seen someone so foreign hesitate before touching the earth itself. His laughter is infectious, and I find myself smiling too, even as I think of the mines buried beneath the soil we’re walking on. The absurdity of it nearly makes me laugh out loud.

That evening, around a fire pit in a courtyard, I listen as the adults speak in Chechen, the words rolling off their tongues like the mountain streams outside. My father translates only snippets, enough to let me know they’re talking about the war, about the years of fighting that still haunt their memories. One woman, her face lined with years of sorrow, looks at me and says something sharp in Chechen. My father stiffens, then turns to me with an apology in his eyes. “She says it’s not safe for you here,” he explains, though I already understand. It’s not me they don’t trust—it’s the language I speak, the passport in my pocket. But then another voice chimes in, a younger man with a cigarette dangling from his lips, and suddenly we’re all laughing again, the tension dissolving like smoke into the night sky.

I don’t sleep well that night. The silence of the mountains is too deep, too full of things left unsaid. But when dawn breaks, I wake to the sound of a donkey braying in the distance and the smell of fresh bread baking in a clay oven. The boy from the mountains is already outside, waiting for me with a grin and a crust of bread in his hand. He doesn’t mention the mines, the war, or the weight of my foreignness. Instead, he just points to the horizon and says, “Come on. There’s a waterfall where the fish are so stupid they jump right into your hands.” And just like that, the land feels less like a place of wounds and more like a place of wonder again. I follow him, my heart lighter, my steps surer, even as I know the shadows are still there, lurking beneath the surface.

I am a dancer. It’s something I’ve only learned recently, but it’s my reality. My story is not one of the typical dancer: I was not the student who couldn’t sit still or pay attention in class, only to find focus and expression through movement. That just isn’t my story. I’ve always been able to sit still, stay engaged, and absorb what my teachers threw at me: I was a “good student”. I would sit at my desk, listen and learn, then go home and do my homework. But, the entire time I embodied that “good student”, I felt like something was missing. It wasn’t physical health—I stayed active and had a healthy diet. But, there was a disconnect between my mind and body. For the longest time, I felt like I lived from the neck up. I love to learn —I always have—but before dance, I was only focused on learning with my head. At the beginning of my junior year I picked up dance. It started on a bit of a whim: I liked watching and I thought learning some moves would help me impress girls. So, I grabbed a like-minded friend and started attending classes. Once I began, I was surprised by how much I liked it. I had discovered something in it that I hadn’t been expecting; I found that I was learning with my entire body.

At first, it was disorienting. I had spent seventeen years treating my body as a vehicle for my brain—something that carried me to class, chewed my food, and occasionally threw a football. Now, suddenly, my body was the one doing the learning. My muscles were memorizing. My feet were thinking. When I fumbled a sequence, it wasn’t because I hadn’t understood the instructions; my head had them perfectly. The failure lived somewhere lower, in my hips, my shoulders, my weight. And the only way to fix it was to feel it, to fail again, to let the correction sink in through repetition rather than explanation.

This was humbling. As a “good student”, I was used to being quick. I could hear something once and own it. Dance refused to work that way. You cannot cram a pirouette. You cannot take notes on rhythm and expect your body to have read them. Progress came slowly, in increments so small I often missed them until someone pointed them out. But when progress did come, it felt earned in a way that an A on a test never had. It lived in me—not in a gradebook, not in a transcript, but in the actual fiber of who I was.

Slowly, the disconnect I had felt for so long began to close. I stopped living from the neck up. I noticed how I carried myself in hallways, how I walked, how I stood in line at the coffee shop. I began to inhabit my body rather than simply operate it. My posture changed. My breathing changed. Even the way I listened to music changed—I stopped hearing songs as background noise and started hearing them as instructions, invitations, blueprints for movement.

The irony is not lost on me: I picked up dance to impress girls, and instead it taught me how to be a whole person. What began as a bit of a whim became the most important education of my junior year. I still love to learn, and I still consider myself a good student. But now the classroom is bigger. It has a floor, mirrors, music, and sweat. Now, when I learn something, I learn it with everything I have—head, heart, and body moving together.

More out of amusement than optimism, I gave it a try. I slid the hanger into the window's seal like I'd seen on crime shows, and spent a few minutes jiggling the apparatus around the inside of the frame. Suddenly, two things simultaneously clicked. One was the lock on the door. (I actually succeeded in springing it.) The other was the realization that I'd been in this type of situation before. In fact, I'd been born into this type of situation. My upbringing has numbed me to unpredictability and chaos. With a family of seven, my home was loud, messy, and spottily supervised. My siblings arguing, the dog barking, the phone ringing—all meant my house was functioning normally. My Dad, a retired Navy pilot, was away half the time. When he was home, he had a parenting style something like a drill sergeant. At the age of nine, I learned how to clear burning oil from the surface of water. My Dad considered this a critical life skill—you know, in case my aircraft carrier should ever get torpedoed. "The water's on fire! Clear a hole!" he shouted, tossing me in the lake without warning.

My Dad's mindset was pure problem-solving: assess the situation, find a tool, act. That was the lesson buried in every chaos bomb he threw at us. When the van lock clicked open, I understood that all those years of improvising—of making dinner from leftovers because Mom forgot to grocery shop, of entertaining my little brother with sock puppets because the power went out again—had trained me for exactly this moment. Not the lock-picking itself, but the shrug, the grin, the "well, someone's got to try" attitude that comes from a lifetime of things not going according to plan.

The college kids cheered. One of them clapped me on the shoulder and said, "Where'd you learn to do that?" I laughed and said something about television, but the honest answer was more complicated. I learned it from a childhood that never sat still. From a mother who turned missed flights into road trips. From a father who believed a crisis was just a problem that hadn't met its match yet. From six siblings who taught me that if you wait for quiet, order, or permission, you'll wait forever.

Growing up, I resented the unpredictability. I wanted the kind of home my friends had—calm, scheduled, predictable, with dinners at the same time every night. I craved normalcy the way some kids crave candy. But standing in that parking lot in Laredo, hanger in hand, feeling the warm Texas evening settle around us, I felt something unexpected: gratitude. My upbringing hadn't just taught me to tolerate chaos; it had taught me to move through it. To laugh in it. To unlock doors in it.

When we finally piled into the van and rolled back toward the work site, I watched the streetlights blur past the window and thought about what was ahead: college, adulthood, a life I couldn't yet imagine. It would be unpredictable. It would be messy. Things would break, plans would fail, doors would lock. And now I knew, with a certainty that surprised me, that I wouldn't panic. I'd find a coat hanger. I'd jiggle it around. I'd take a breath, take a step back, and figure it out. My Dad would be proud—probably of the lock, but definitely of the shrug.

During our summers in Oregon, instead of renting a car, we pedaled through the hilly streets on a three-person bike. If we were lucky, we got to end the day at a high mountain hut where we drank endless cups of rich hot chocolate. I would sit in the corner of the dining room engrossed in books about rare lichen.

At the top of that final peak, the one I had chased all summer, I sat on a cairn of rocks and let my legs dangle over the edge of the world. The White Mountains stretched out beneath me in every direction, a patchwork of green and granite that seemed to go on forever. My father, who had joined me for the last climb despite his bad knee, handed me a granola bar and said nothing. He didn't need to. We both knew what this moment meant.

On a road bike, the bars will typically be an inch or two below the saddle; on a more upright machine, level with it or slightly above. There is no single correct position, but there are many wrong ones, and the wrong ones tend to announce themselves over time: numb hands, aching shoulders, a neck that complains on every long ride.

Do not be seduced by the idea that a bigger frame is somehow more serious. Here is an article that quantifies the heat loss effects of cotton, polyester and polypropylene: Rossi et al., Dry and Wet Heat Transfer Through Clothing Dependent on the Clothing Properties Under Cold Conditions , International Journal of Occupational Safety and Ergonomics (JOSE) 2008, Vol. 14, No. 1, 69–76. Here is a rough summary of their experimental setup so you can understand the applicability and limitations to real-life scenarios. Test on a human manikin which simulates body heating and sweating. The clothing was fit similarly between materials as much as possible and consisted of underwear covering upper body and legs Clothing consisted of an inner layer (cotton, polyester, or polypropylene) and an outer layer (categorized by being impermeable, semi-permeable, and permeable to moisture). This two-layer system more accurately simulates real life layering. (You probably aren't just going out in the cold in a t-shirt). Here is the information on the materials: The amount of sweat produced by the manikin is kept constant for all trials (550 g) The length of time per trial is 2.5 hrs, under steady-state conditions, with an ambient temperature of 10 C. Not specifically stated, but I believe overall heat loss rates are measured by the manikin (how much heat required to keep the manikin at a certain temperature). The change in mass of each layer was measured after the experiment to determine how much moisture was absorbed. Cotton contains almost 4x the amount of water as polypropylene (a much more hydrophobic material). Also note that more of the water is contained right at the skin layer for polypropylene and polyester. The outer layer makes the biggest difference in where the moisture goes, with semi-permeable and permeable outer layers resulting in most of the water being evaporated.

In other words, the inner layer’s job is not to keep you dry in any absolute sense, but to manage where the moisture ends up. Cotton holds onto that moisture, and because it holds it right against your skin, you get the familiar cold, clammy feeling once you stop moving. Polypropylene and polyester, being hydrophobic, don’t absorb much water at all, so the sweat tends to stay as liquid water at the skin surface rather than being taken up into the fabric itself. That sounds worse at first, but it means the moisture is available to be moved outward and evaporated if the outer layer permits it. This is where the two-layer system matters. A permeable or semi-permeable outer layer lets that vapor escape, so the water leaves the system entirely rather than accumulating. An impermeable outer layer traps it, and then it doesn’t matter much what your base layer is made of, because the moisture has nowhere to go.

The practical upshot is that the common advice to avoid cotton in cold, wet conditions is well supported, but the reason is subtler than “cotton gets wet.” All of these materials get wet when you sweat. The difference is whether the water is held in the fabric, close to the skin, where it conducts heat away from your body, or whether it can be transported outward and evaporated. Cotton’s high absorptive capacity means it acts as a reservoir of moisture right where you least want one. Synthetics shed that role, but they only shine when paired with an outer layer that breathes. If your shell is impermeable, you’ve defeated the advantage of the synthetic base layer.

A few caveats are worth keeping in mind. The manikin produces a constant 550 g of sweat over 2.5 hours, which is a moderate, steady output, not the burst you get from sprinting to catch a bus, nor the low-level trickle of a leisurely walk. Real people vary their sweat rate, remove layers, open zippers, and stop and start. The study also held ambient temperature at 10 °C, which is chilly but not extreme, and it didn’t account for wind, which dramatically increases convective heat loss regardless of fabric. So treat the findings as a clean comparison of material behavior under controlled conditions, not a universal ranking. Still, the core lesson holds: in the cold, what you wear closest to your skin and what you wear over it work as a system, and the outer layer often decides whether your base layer helps or hurts.

"Accelerate instantly" would imply that a photon takes many different velocities at the same point in time. In fact, it would imply that a photon takes on every velocity between $0$ and $c$ simultaneously , but that clearly makes no sense at all - a particle cannot have many instantaneous velocities simultaneously. When a photon is created, it is traveling at $c$ . A photon is always traveling at $c$ , there is no such thing as a stationary photon which is then accelerated.

The very notion of accelerating a photon is therefore incoherent. You cannot take something that has no rest frame, no moment of stillness, and speak of it gaining speed. It is born at $c$ , it lives at $c$ , and it dies at $c$ , never once deviating from that singular velocity in any inertial frame. What changes when light passes through a medium is not the speed of the photons themselves but the effective phase velocity of the light, a subtlety often lost in casual conversation. So the phrase "accelerate instantly" is doubly wrong: it presumes a before and an after, a slow state and a fast state, when in truth there is only ever one speed, and it is always the same.

The expression is quite old as a term for sightseeing, and appears to have originated in the form "see the lions." J.S. Farmer & W.E. Henley, Slang and Its Analogues Past and Present (1896) has this entry for the earlier term: Lion , subs. (old). ... 2. (colloquial).—An object (animate or inanimate) of interest. To SEE THE LIONS = to go sightseeing. [First three cited examples:] 1590 Greene, Never Too Late {Grosart,viii,68} This country Francesco was no other but a meere nouice, and that so newly, that to use the old proverb, he had scarce SEENE THE LIONS. 1785. Grose, Vulg. Tongue , s.v. Lion ... to SHOW THE LIONS and tombs, to point out the particular curiosities of any place,an allusion to Westminster Abbey and the Tower where the tombs and lions are shown. ... It is a standing joke among the city wits to send boys and country-folks on the first of April to the Tower ditch to see the lions washed. The Greene reference is to " the Palmer's Story " in Robert Greene, Never Too Late (1590): "This courtisan, seeing this countrey Francesco was no other but a meere nouice, and that so newly that, to vse the old prouerb, he had scarce seene the lions, she thought to intrap him and so arrest him with her amorous glances that shee would wring him by the pursse : wherevpon euery day shee would out at hir casement stand, and there discouer her beauties.” Evidently "to see the lions" was already an old proverb in 1590.

The Tower of London maintained a royal menagerie from at least the thirteenth century, and it is this collection of actual lions that gave the phrase its literal anchor. For centuries, the lions were among the chief attractions of London for visitors from the provinces and abroad, and "showing the lions" became a recognized occupation. The keepers charged admission, and the phrase "lion's fee" appears in various records of the period as the standard charge for viewing the beasts. Samuel Pepys visited the menagerie in 1660 and recorded the experience in his diary, noting among other things that a lion there bore a striking resemblance to one of his acquaintances, which he took as an amusing coincidence.

The menagerie remained open to the public until 1835, when the animals were transferred to the Zoological Society's gardens in Regent's Park, partly on account of an accident in which a lion injured a keeper. With the departure of the actual lions, the figurative sense was left standing on its own, and "lion" came to mean any celebrated person or noteworthy object. Hence the later expression "a literary lion," applied to authors who were the darlings of fashionable society, and the still-current "lionize," meaning to treat someone as a celebrity.

The transition from literal beasts to figurative celebrities seems to have occurred gradually over the eighteenth century. By the time Boswell was making his celebrated visits to London, he could speak of being introduced to the great men of the age in terms that suggest the lions of the Tower had become the lions of the drawing room. Dr. Johnson himself appears in one of Boswell's anecdotes using the word in this transferred sense, and from that period onward the usage was firmly established.

What is striking is how long the phrase endured in its older form. As late as the middle of the nineteenth century, writers were using "see the lions" without any sense of archaism, and guidebooks of the period routinely promised readers the principal lions of each town they might pass through. The phrase has since faded from common use, surviving chiefly in "lionize" and in the historical sense of a "lion" as an object of fashionable curiosity. But its origin remains a small monument to the days when the most famous beasts in England were kept not in a zoo but in a fortress, and seeing them was the height of every visitor's ambition.

As others have said, downvoted posts aren't deleted; they're hidden if they've been downvoted too much. But there's another aspect as well. It certainly *can* contribute to a "hivemind" mentality, but it has another very important function: It allows those who prefer not to post, because they either cannot be bothered, aren't very eloquent or not good at rhetorics, to have a significant impact on a discussion. If you look at other messaging boards that do not feature a voting system, generally speaking the people who are the loudest (e.g. spam the most walls of text) are the ones who get heard and these people can easily verbally overpower those who aren't as "loud".

A voting system gives a voice to the silent majority, so to speak, and that's a valuable thing. It's not a perfect system, of course — it can be gamed, brigaded, and it can absolutely reinforce existing biases. But the alternative, where only those willing to write lengthy replies get to shape the conversation, has its own serious problems. Those who write the most aren't necessarily the ones with the best arguments; they're just the ones with the most time, energy, or stubbornness. A downvote is a quick, low-effort way for a casual reader to say "I disagree" or "this isn't helpful" without having to compose a rebuttal. That's not laziness; it's accessibility. The real issue isn't the existence of voting, but how people interpret it — treating a score as a measure of truth rather than a rough signal of community sentiment.

While there, pick up every bit of knowledge that you can. Find out how you can get into that next spot and work for it. Learn from the people who do it. Get to know them on a personal level. When a spot opens up, jump on it. Those people who you have been talking to will vouch for you if you proved yourself. It is a series of stepping stones. They are going to be small steps and will require a lot of work. I had no IT experience when I landed my first job as a helpdesk agent assisting hotel guests in connecting to the internet at their hotel.

and I fumbled through those early days like a newborn fawn—until I realized the real lesson wasn’t tech, but patience. Every "stupid" question I asked or system I broke became part of a quiet ledger, one that said, “This kid’s willing to show up.” Years later, when that same chain promoted me to tier-two support, my manager didn’t promote me because of some certificate or polished LinkedIn post; she vouched for me because she’d seen me stay late rewiring routers in closets or staying patient with a furious executive who couldn’t print. Doors open when they recognize the grind behind the polish.

I work in a dentist's office in the US, and this is exaggerated at best. Most dental insurances are PPO plans, which are fee-for-service (as opposed to DMO or DHMO, which is managed care). Fee-for-service means that you/your insurance are charged for each procedure completed, not a standard fee for just visiting the office and seeing your dentist. So no, your co-pay does not appear on your card, but your coverage percentages might. Dental coverage is often broken down into preventative (cleanings, x-rays, exams)/basic (fillings, root canals, periodontics)/major (crowns, bridges, dentures) percentages, the most common breakdown being 100/80/50. If your dentist participates with your insurance plan (is in-network), they have to write off a portion of their fee to the maximum allowable charge by the insurance (they should have a fee schedule on file from the insurance as to what they are allowed to charge).

If they are out-of-network, they can charge whatever they want, and your insurance will reimburse you based on their usual, customary, and reasonable (UCR) rates, which may leave you with a larger balance. That’s why the same crown can cost you $300 at one office and $900 at another. Annual maximums are also a huge factor—most plans cap out around $1,000 to $1,500 per year, which hasn’t changed much since the 1970s. So when people say dental insurance is a scam, I get the frustration, but it’s really more of a coupon book than true insurance. It helps, but it was never designed to cover everything, and it definitely wasn’t designed to be simple.

American Indians still exist, but many of them just look like regular white people these days. A half black person is obviously black. (outside of a couple places in the southwest) Native children were taken from their homes by white settlers and placed into "indian schools", the purpose of which was to strip them of their native customs. There, they were often assaulted as punishment for partaking in "non-white" customs.

This practice wasn’t as long ago as people like to think, either. It continued well into the twentieth century, and the last of those schools didn’t close until the nineties. So you have generations of native people who were raised to be ashamed of their own culture, taught that their languages were backward and their ceremonies were savage. That kind of thing doesn’t just wash out in a generation or two. It lingers. It shapes how families talk to each other, or don’t. It shapes what gets passed down and what gets buried. So when someone says they’ve never met a real Indian, what they usually mean is they’ve never met someone who fits the costume they saw in a John Wayne movie.

The core friction here isn't about suppressing ideas, but about managing liability and brand safety in a volatile cultural landscape. If a creator realizes their work inadvertently aligns with a tragedy or a social movement they didn’t anticipate, forcing them to maintain the original text is arguably less respectful than allowing them to revise it. Art is not static; it exists in conversation with its audience and context. When that context shifts violently, insisting on immutability can feel like prioritizing ego over empathy.

Critics will scream slippery slopes, arguing that this opens the door to retroactive erasure of history or unpopular truths. But there is a distinct line between historical documentation and commercial entertainment. A documentary recording a protest should remain untouched because its value lies in factual preservation. A fictional narrative sold for entertainment carries different obligations. The producer holds the copyright, not just as an artistic right, but as a commercial asset. They have the legal and moral prerogative to alter their product if they deem the current version harmful to their bottom line or their community’s well-being.

Furthermore, we must acknowledge the power dynamics inherent in "free speech." Political censorship is state-sanctioned violence against expression. Economic censorship is merely the market saying, "We don't want to buy this specific configuration of pixels." These are fundamentally different mechanisms. One silences dissent through force; the other adjusts supply based on demand. Conflating them dilutes the seriousness of actual authoritarian control. If we treat every corporate decision to edit content as equivalent to a government banning books, we lose the ability to identify real threats to liberty. We become paralyzed by false equivalencies, unable to distinguish between a tyrant’s decree and a studio’s risk management strategy. Ultimately, if you don't like what the corporation sells, you have the freedom not to buy it. That is the true essence of economic freedom, not the guarantee that every commercial product will remain unchanged forever.

Yes, I had trouble with this as well. The thing that helped me was to realise what a big difference there is between many-one reducibility and polynomial-time Turing reducibility. (These different types of reducibility are sometimes called “Karp reducible” and “Cook reducible” respectively. I have read that is a misrepresentation of what Cook and Karp actually did, but even if that’s true these terms are very widely used so you need to know what people mean by them.) Many-one reducibility is very restricted.

With many-one reducibility, you get one shot: you must transform your instance of problem A into a single instance of problem B, and then the answer to B's instance must be exactly the answer to A's instance. That's it. No questions asked in the middle, no adaptivity, no combining of several answers.

Polynomial-time Turing reducibility, by contrast, is far more generous. You get to run B as an oracle as many times as you like, provided the total time is polynomial, and you can choose later queries based on earlier answers. So you can, for instance, ask several questions and take a majority vote, or use B to compute some intermediate quantity that isn't itself an answer to any instance of A.

This difference matters enormously. If A many-one reduces to B and B is in P, then A is in P — that's easy. But if A only Turing reduces to B and B is in P, you still get A in P, so for decidability questions the two notions behave similarly. The real divergence shows up in complexity classes like NP: it is far from obvious whether everything in NP Turing-reduces to SAT in the same strong sense.

I lived in Arizona for 18 years, so let me enlighten you. There is barely any water and very little vegetation, true, but the plants and animals that evolved to live in the desert rely on the little water that they get. Arizona (at least the southern half) gets less than 15 inches of rain per year. Half of that comes during the monsoons of early summer. It is during this time that the water table under the desert is replenished. This in turn provides the water to most of the native plant life for much of the year. Additionally, many of the native desert plants store water for the long term. Most have evolved to hold enough water to survive the dry fall and winter, and need to replenish their supply in the spring with the first rains.

When that rain doesn’t come, the effects are more serious than a brown lawn or a few dying shrubs. Saguaros, mesquite, creosote, and all the other plants that make up the desert ecosystem are part of a delicate balance. They provide food and shade for animals, stabilize the soil, and help the land recover after a dry spell. If they are removed or replaced with plants that need constant irrigation, the strain on the water supply grows, and the native ecosystem loses ground.

People sometimes assume that because desert plants are adapted to drought, they can be neglected indefinitely. That isn’t quite true. Adapted does not mean invulnerable. A prolonged drought, especially when combined with development and groundwater pumping, can push even well-adapted plants past their limits. Some of them take decades to grow, so once they’re gone, they don’t come back quickly.

The desert is beautiful, but it is not empty, and its water is not an unlimited resource. If you live there, it makes sense to choose native plants, water sparingly, and understand that the landscape has its own needs. We can’t make Arizona into a wetter place by wishing it so; we can only learn to live within the conditions that are already there.
